The forward noising process has been implemented following Section 2.2
The drift term for VESDE is defined as $f(x, t)=0$
The diffusion term for VESDE is defined as $g(t)=\sigma_{min} \cdot (\frac{\sigma_{min}}{\sigma_{max}})^t \cdot \sqrt{2 \log \frac{\sigma_{max}}{\sigma_{min}}}$
The constant $\sigma_{\text{min}}$ for VESDE is set to 0.01 for the tasks SIR and Two Moons
The constant $\sigma_{\text{min}}$ for VESDE is set to 0.05 for the tasks Gaussian Linear, Gaussian Mixture, Gaussian Linear Uniform, Bernoulli GLM, SLCP, and Lotka Volterra

The constant $\sigma_{\text{max}}$ for VESDE is chosen to be as large as the maximum Euclidean distance between all pairs of training data points for the current task. For sequential methods, the training data points that are used are the training data points available in the first round
The time interval used in VESDE is (0, 1]
The drift term for VPSDE is defined as $f(x, t)=-\frac{1}{2}\beta_t\theta_t$, where $\beta_t = \beta_{\text{min}} + t(\beta_{\text{max}} - \beta_{\text{min}})$
The diffusion term for VPSDE is defined as $\sqrt{\beta_t}$, where $\beta_t = \beta_{\text{min}} + t(\beta_{\text{max}} - \beta_{\text{min}})$
The constant $\beta_\text{min}$ for VPSDE is set to 0.1
The constant $\beta_\text{max}$ for VPSDE is set to 11.0
The time interval used in VPSDE is (0, 1]
Code has been implemented for VESDE to compute the (gradients of the) transition log density
Code has been implemented for VPSDE to compute the (gradients of the) transition log density
The sbibm library is used to implement Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE)
Code is implemented to train Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) using the sbibm library
The sbibm library is used to implement Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation (SNPE)
Code is implemented to train Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation (SNPE) using the sbibm library
Truncated Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation (TSNPE) is implemented using the GitHub repo https://github.com/mackelab/tsnpe_neurips
C2ST has been implemented using the default implementation from `sbibm`, using default hyperparameters
When training NPSE, for each sampled parameter from the prior $\theta_0$, code is implemented to use the simulator to generate a corresponding observation $x$; $x \sim p(x|theta_0)$
When training NPSE, for each $\theta_0$ and corresponding observation $x$, code is implemented to simulate the forward diffusion process using an SDE to obtain $\theta_t$ at time $t$

When training NPSE, code is implemented to compute the loss as a Monte Carlo estimate of $\left\| s_\psi(\theta_t, x, t) - \nabla_{\theta_t} \log p_t(\theta_t | \theta) \right\|^2$, where $s_\psi(\theta_t, x, t)$ is the result of the score network, and $\nabla_{\theta_t} \log p_{t \mid 0}(\theta_t \mid \theta_0)$ is the forward diffusion transition log density
When sampling using NPSE, samples are drawn from the stationary distribution $\pi$ (unit gaussian distribution); $\overline{\theta}_0 \sim \pi(\cdot)$

When sampling using NPSE, the approximation of the time-reversal of the probability flow ODE is implemented given some observation $x = x_{\text{obs}}$, and replacing the score of the (perturbed) posterior(s) with the neural network; $\nabla_\theta \log p_t(\theta \vert x_{\text{obs}}) \approx s_\psi(\theta_t, x_{\text{obs}}, t)$. RK45 is used to solve the ODE
In TSNPSE, given a total budget of $N$ simulations and $R$ rounds, the simulations are evenly distributed across rounds; the number of simulations per round $M$ is computed as $M=N/R$
In TSNPSE, the initial proposal prior is equivalent to the known prior of the current task; $p(\theta) =: p^{-0}(\theta)$

In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, after applying the NPSE algorithm to learn a score network, 20000 samples are simulated from the approximate posterior via (the time-reversal of) the probability flow ODE using the neural network approximation of $\nabla_\theta \log p_t(\theta \vert x_{\text{obs}})$
In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, the (approximate) likelihood $p(\theta \mid x_{\text{obs}})$ of the samples under the model is computed using the instantaneous-change-of-variables formula

In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, the truncation boundary is computed as the $\epsilon = 5 \times 10^{-4}$-th percentile of the samples from the approximate posterior. This defines the log-probability rejection threshold for rejection sampling.
In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, when sampling from the truncated proposal prior, samples are first drawn from the prior as $\theta \sim p(\theta)$.

In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, when sampling from the truncated proposal prior, an initial rejection step is applied to samples drawn from the prior; the samples are rejected if they do not belong to the empirical hyperrectangle defined by the approximate posterior samples. That is, the hyperrectangle defined as the Cartesian product of the one-dimensional intervals with endpoints given by the minimum and maximum of the approximate posterior samples in each dimension.

In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, when sampling from the truncated proposal prior, following the initial rejection step, the likelihood of the samples from the prior under the approximate posterior is computed using the instantaneous change-of-variables formula.

In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, when sampling from the truncated proposal prior, samples are accepted if the likelihood under the approximation posterior is greater than the truncation boundary that has been computed on the $r$-th round. Otherwise they are rejected.
In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, when sampling from the truncated proposal prior, the previous steps are repeated until the required number of samples from the proposal prior have been obtained.

In TSNPSE, in the $r$-th round, a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of $|M|$ samples is constructed by drawing $\theta_i \sim {p}^{-r-1}(\theta)$, $x_i \sim p(x \mid \theta_i)$, and adding $(\theta_i, x_i)$ to $\mathcal{D}$, where ${p}^{-r-1}(\theta)$ denotes the proposal prior and $p(x|\theta)$ denotes the simulator.

In TSNPSE, in each of the rounds, given a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of $|M|$ samples, the NPSE algorithm is followed to learn a neural network which approximates the score(s) of the perturbed posterior(s) $\nabla_{\theta_t} \log p_t(\theta_t | x)$

In TSNPSE, the score network computed in the final round is used as the final approximation of the scores $\nabla_{\theta_t} \log p_t(\theta_t | x)$, and can be used to generate approximate samples from the posterior, as per the standard NPSE algorithm
The parameter embedding network $\theta_t$ is a 3-layer fully-connected MLP with 256 hidden units in each layer.
The output dimension from the final layer of the parameter embedding network is determined by $\max (30, 4 \cdot d)$, where $d$ is the input dimension to the parameter embedding network
The observation embedding network $\x$ is a 3-layer fully-connected MLP with 256 hidden units in each layer
The output dimension from the final layer of the observation embedding network is determined by $\max (30, 4 \cdot p)$, where $p$ is the input dimension to the observation embedding network
The sinusoidal embedding $t$ is embedded into 64 dimensions

The sinusoidal embedding $t$ is computed as follows: the $i$-th value is computed as $\sin \left( \frac{t}{10000^{(i-1)/31}} \right)$ if $i \leq 32$, otherwise it is computed as $\cos \left( \frac{t}{10000^{((i-32)-1)/31}} \right)$
The score network is a 3-layer fully-connected MLP with 256 hidden units in each layer

Both the output of the parameter embedding network $\theta_t$ and output of the observation embedding network $x$ are standardized before being inputted to the score network, by subtracting an estimate of the mean and dividing by the standard deviation in each dimension. The empirical mean and empirical standard deviation of the training data is used

The score network takes the concatenated input $[\theta_{\text{emb}}, x_{\text{emb}}, t_{\text{emb}}] $, i.e. the outputs of the parameter embedding network, the output of the observation embedding network, and the output of the sinusoidal embedding network concatenated together
The output dimension of the score network is equal to the dimension of the parameter embedding network
All MLP networks use SiLU activation functions between layers
Adam is used as the optimizer to train all networks
A learning rate of 10^-4 is used when training all networks
15% of each dataset is held out as a validation split. In sequential experiments, the validation split is re-computed on every round as 15% of the available simulations sampled uniformly at random

After each training step the loss on the validation split is computed. If this validation loss doesn't decrease for 1000 steps, then training is stopped and the network that gave the lowest validation loss is returned
The maximum number of training iterations is 3000
For experiments with a simulation budget of either 1000 or 10000, the batch size is 50 for non-sequential experiments (NPSE-VE, NPSE-VP, NPE)
For experiments with a simulation budget of either 1000 or 10000, the batch size is 200 for sequential experiments (TSNPSE-VE, TSNPSE-VP, SNPE, TSNPE)
For simulation budgets of 100000 the batch size is 500 for all tasks
When computing the C2ST score, 10000 samples from both the true posterior and the approximate posterior are used
For each simulation budget 10^3, 10^4, 10^5, all non-sequential methods (NPSE-VE, NPSE-VP, NPE) have been trained on all tasks and evaluated using C2ST
For each simulation budget 10^3, 10^4, 10^5, all sequential methods (TSNPSE-VE, TSNPSE-VP, SNPE, TSNPE) have been trained for 10 rounds on all tasks and evaluated using C2ST

The percentage of valid summary statistics from each method is computed after each round, where an invalid summary statistic is when the Pyloric simulator returns a `NaN` (in one or more of the output dimensions)
A posterior mean-predictive sample is computed at the end of the final round, by first computing the mean of the approximate posterior samples, then acquiring a simulation
The recorded metrics show that, in the final round, SNPSE-VP achieves about 80% valid summary statistics
